But "it depends" is useless without the decision framework, so here is the one that actually settles it, followed by what each path looks like in 2026. The three questions that decide it 1. Enterprise-heavy markets and Microsoft shops lean Azure. Startups, product companies, and most of the global market lean AWS.

articles.title: The Name It Hears
articles.excerpt: The Name It Hears I said “hey Hearthlen” from the next machine. The ThinkPad microphone recorded it, and the wake listener did nothing. Savindu Thathsara, savithathsara.me. This is a Hearthlen note fr…
articles.body: The Name It Hears I said “hey Hearthlen” from the next machine. The ThinkPad microphone recorded it, and the wake listener did nothing. Savindu Thathsara, savithathsara.me . This is a Hearthlen note from the two computers sitting together. The old listener was PocketSphinx, waiting for “hey hearth” and “hard one”, because that is what an English dictionary makes of a made-up name. On this recording Whisper heard “Hey, Hertzland.” The keyword list, at its most sensitive setting, scored 0 hits. The listener now transcribes a short burst and accepts the name as it actually comes out: hearthlin, herthlin, hertzland. The burst that woke it took 340 ms . The log line was wake: hey hearthlen , one second after the phrase ended, and it gave the greeting.

articles.title: Once tokens cost cents, your agent bill runs on minutes
articles.excerpt: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 resolves a SWE benchmark task for just under 20 cents in tokens. At that price, the bill that matters is wall-clock time: sandboxes, CI runners, concurrency slots and people w…
articles.body: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 resolves a SWE benchmark task for just under 20 cents in tokens. At that price, the bill that matters is wall-clock time: sandboxes, CI runners, concurrency slots and people waiting. cost per task ≈ token_cost + wall_clock_hours x hourly_rate_of_everything_waiting Three things change once you price time: The host matters as much as the model. Same MIT weights, OpenRouter hosts ranging from 24 to 290 tokens per second, prices barely tracking it. Concurrency follows wall clock. At 1,000 tasks an hour, a 7.6 minute task (210 tok/s) needs about 127 slots. The same task at 42 tok/s takes 23.5 minutes and needs about 392. Success rate divides everything. 8 minutes at 55% success is roughly even with 12 minutes at 85%.

articles.title: Letting AI Write Code Against Your Drawings: The mlightcad MCP Server
articles.excerpt: Stop teaching AI 100 CAD tools. Give it a scripting API and let it figure things out. A few weeks ago, I published Building a CAD Agent: MCP, Tools, or Let AI Write Code?. The basic argument was simpl…
articles.body: Stop teaching AI 100 CAD tools. Give it a scripting API and let it figure things out. A few weeks ago, I published Building a CAD Agent: MCP, Tools, or Let AI Write Code? . The basic argument was simple: For complex software like CAD, giving AI a scripting API is often better than giving it a shopping list of tools. Think about it. If you want an AI agent to work with a CAD drawing, you could give it tools like: draw_line draw_circle query_entities set_entity_layer delete_entity Sounds reasonable, right? Until someone asks: "Find all circles near standard bolt-hole sizes, ignore reference layers, group them by component, flag unusual ones, and generate a report." Oops. Looks like we need another tool. And another. And another.

articles.body: The modern workplace is no longer defined by desks, meeting rooms, and office equipment alone. Technology has become part of the physical environment, influencing how employees communicate, use shared spaces, manage daily tasks, and interact with the building itself. This shift has created a new generation of workplaces where digital systems and physical design operate together. From cloud platforms and wireless networks to smart sensors and automated lighting, technology is changing both how offices function and how they are designed. Smart Technology Is Becoming Part of Office Infrastructure In traditional offices, technology was often treated as a separate layer. Computers, phones, and network equipment were added after the physical workspace had already been designed.

Every number below is re-derived from raw counts in a sealed container, and the spot-checks were fetched live so you can repeat them. When a PyPI project ships a README, it should declare how to render it with one metadata field, Description-Content-Type , surfaced as info.description_content_type : text/markdown , text/x-rst , or text/plain . articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
